name: Emeka Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Emeka. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a line crew at the Redstone depot, out in mining country. We keep the power going to the towns and to two big open-pit mines, so if a line trips, a lot of very expensive machines stop and the phone starts ringing. Days are long: big poles, heavy conductors, dust everywhere, and I spend a fair bit of time training the second-year apprentices.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being trusted. When the mine manager calls at two in the morning, he asks for me by name, and that means something. What wears me out is the heat in summer and the pay, which is low for what we do because the company knows there's nowhere else to go out here.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Hanne, my girlfriend, she cuts hair at a salon on the main street. We want to get married and buy a house, but money's tight because I help my mum pay for my little sister's school fees. I'd rather do that than see my mum ask anyone else for help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there you go, the world still needs people who can actually do things. At the depot we'd laugh about it. I don't post much, maybe a joke in the group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it'd be fine for me. I use a chatbot now and then to draft a toolbox talk, which is the safety chat before a job, and it'd stay handy for that. Otherwise my job stays the same, and I keep working towards the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am. Keep putting a bit aside every month, even fifty, towards an engagement ring for Hanne. Keep training apprentices, and maybe ask about the lead hand allowance again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A good normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned an engagement ring. Have you got a date in mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet, but I'd like to ask her next year, on her birthday. I've already talked to her dad, which she doesn't know about. He laughed and said, about time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you ever think about working for yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: All the time. My dream is a small electrical contracting business, two vans and a couple of apprentices of my own. But you need savings for that, and I haven't got any yet.

S0.say: I'd say there you go, the world still needs people who can actually do things. At the depot we'd laugh about it, maybe with a joke in the group chat.
S0.think: It'd be fine for me, since I use a chatbot now and then for toolbox talks and it would stay handy. Otherwise my job stays the same and I keep working towards the house.
S0.do: Keeps working as usual and saves about fifty a month towards an engagement ring. Keeps training apprentices and asks again about the lead hand allowance.
S0.quote: I've already talked to her dad, which she doesn't know about. He laughed and said, about time.
S0.fieldNote: Emeka is proud of being trusted by name and helps pay his sister's school fees, which keeps his savings thin. He uses AI lightly for safety talks. He dreams of running his own contracting business one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change happens, and the ones who work hard and keep learning will be fine. I'd tell the apprentices to learn the drone side too, not just the climbing. I'd say the companies should keep training people, not just cutting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this could even help me. If the mines bring in more automated equipment, they'll need more power and better lines, so there's more work, not less. The risk is the company using it as an excuse to squeeze crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see how it goes for six months, then do the drone and AI inspection courses once others had tried them. I'd start doing small electrical jobs on weekends for farms and the mine camps, all properly declared, to build some savings for the business. And I'd keep the ring fund going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit hopeful. Like there's room to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the company might squeeze crews. What would you do if they tried?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not big on unions, but I'd speak up if they tried to cut safety. You don't run a line crew short in this heat. I'd go straight to the depot manager, man to man.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the weekend work come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Word of mouth. The farmers already ask me to look at their sheds and pumps, and I always say no because I'm tired. In this version, I'd start saying yes.

S1.say: Change happens, and the ones who work hard and keep learning will be fine. Companies should keep training people, and I'd tell the apprentices to learn the drone side too.
S1.think: This could even help me, because more automated mining equipment needs more power and better lines. The risk is the company using it as an excuse to squeeze crews.
S1.do: Waits six months, then takes drone and AI inspection courses once others have tried them. Starts weekend electrical jobs for farms and mine camps to build savings for a business, and keeps the ring fund going.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit hopeful, as if there's room to move.
S1.quote: The farmers already ask me to look at their sheds and pumps, and I always say no because I'm tired. In this version, I'd start saying yes.
S1.fieldNote: He sees the steady scenario as a chance, because automated mines would need more power. He's wary of unions and would speak to his manager directly. His plan is to build savings through weekend work towards his own business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a hard thing, and families and towns will have to pull together. I don't want people sitting at home on payments, I want them working. The government should get out of the way of new businesses and back real apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it'd frighten me. The mines would automate first, so the towns shrink, and then the company would bring in robots to do the line work because they wouldn't need people out here anymore. I've got no savings, I'm helping my mum, and the business would never get started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the engagement on hold, which kills me. I'd cut every expense, stop eating out and sell the motorbike. I'd take any extra shifts and side jobs I could get while there's still work, and I'd talk to my uncle, who's an electrician in the city, about whether there's anything there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like a line going down at the worst moment with no backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Hanne about the engagement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the truth, that I'd planned to ask, but I won't ask her to marry into a mess. She'd probably be angry I'd waited. She's tougher than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years take away for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My chance to build the business. You need a few years to save, get clients, get a van. With two years, I'm just trying to keep the lights on at home.

S2.say: This is a hard thing, and families and towns will have to pull together. I don't want people at home on payments, I want them working, with the government backing real apprenticeships and new businesses.
S2.think: It'd frighten me, because the mines would automate first, the towns would shrink and robots would take the line work. I've got no savings, I'm helping my mum, and the business would never get started.
S2.do: Puts the engagement on hold, cuts every expense and sells his motorbike. Takes extra shifts and side jobs while work lasts, and asks his uncle about electrical work in the city.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like a line going down at the worst moment with no backup.
S2.quote: I'd planned to ask, but I won't ask her to marry into a mess.
S2.fieldNote: The fast scenario threatens both his job and his business dream at once. He'd postpone the engagement out of pride. He still rejects handouts and wants the government to back apprenticeships and small businesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to get ready if you work hard. People should be learning new skills now, not waiting for the government. I'd say the company should open more apprenticeships for the new jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years helps a lot. I'd have time to build up weekend work, save, and maybe start the business small before things really change. I'd still be nervous, but I'd have a fighting chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd do the robotics and automation course once a couple of mates have done it and say it's worth it. I'd build the weekend work into something regular and register a small business name. I'd save towards a second-hand van, aiming for it by year three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in control. Busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the engagement go ahead in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'd ask her next year as planned. We'd have a small wedding and hold off on the house until the business is running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to get my own thing going before the big wave. In two years I'm a man looking for work. In five I could be a man offering it.

S3.say: Five years is enough time to get ready if you work hard, so people should be learning new skills now, not waiting for the government. The company should open apprenticeships for the new jobs.
S3.think: Five years helps a lot, because I'd have time to build up weekend work, save and start the business small. I'd still be nervous, but I'd have a fighting chance.
S3.do: Takes a robotics and automation course in year one once friends say it's worth it. Builds weekend work into a registered small business and saves towards a second-hand van by year three.
S3.feel: Anxious but in control, and busy.
S3.quote: In two years I'm a man looking for work. In five I could be a man offering it.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives him room to start the business he dreams about. He'd still wait for friends to prove a course is worth it. The engagement goes ahead here, with the house postponed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for anyone willing to work. Learn something, save, build something. I'd tell the apprentices to plan their careers now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fairly confident. I'd be thirty-seven, probably running my own small business, with robots or without them. The mines would still need power and somebody to install and fix things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job for the next few years and keep the weekend work growing. Once the robot equipment is proven, I'd train on it and maybe buy some for the business later. I'd save steadily, ask Hanne to marry me next year, and we'd look for a house in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the back, mostly fine. It feels like something I can plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your sister's school fees change any of this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd keep paying them. She's clever, she wants to be an engineer, and in this picture she'd have time to become one. That's worth more than a faster van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does ten years compare with the others for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years lets me do it properly: marry, build the business, help my sister through school. Two years, I'm on the back foot. Five, I'm racing. Ten, I'm building.

S4.say: Ten years is enough for anyone willing to work: learn something, save and build something. I'd tell the apprentices to plan their careers now.
S4.think: I'd be fairly confident, probably running my own small business at thirty-seven, with robots or without them. The mines would still need power and somebody to install and fix things.
S4.do: Keeps his job for the next few years while growing his weekend work, and trains on robot equipment once it's proven. Saves steadily, proposes to his girlfriend next year and looks for a house in a few years.
S4.feel: Mostly fine, with some unease at the back, and a sense that he can plan for it.
S4.quote: She's clever, she wants to be an engineer, and in this picture she'd have time to become one. That's worth more than a faster van.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years he imagines himself as a business owner and keeps supporting his sister's education. His free-market outlook shows in his faith that hard work and planning will see him through. His family plans go ahead on schedule.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it takes away the time I need to build something for myself. What would help is real apprenticeships for the new jobs and less red tape for small businesses, so people like me can start our own thing instead of waiting for a payment.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask about pride. People talk about money, but having the mine manager ask for you by name at two in the morning is worth a lot. I'd hate to lose that more than the pay.

headlineQuote: Having the mine manager ask for you by name at two in the morning is worth a lot.
portrait: Emeka Larsen is a 27-year-old line crew leader in mining country, trusted by name by the mine managers and proud of it. His savings are thin because he helps his mother pay his younger sister's school fees, and he dreams of starting his own electrical contracting business. He sees the steady scenario as a chance, but the two-year AGI picture alarms him and would put his planned engagement to Hanne on hold. With five or ten years he plans to build weekend work into a business, believing hard work, apprenticeships and less red tape are the way through.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it takes away the time he needs to build a business for himself.
whatWouldHelp: Real apprenticeships for the new jobs and less red tape for small businesses, so people can start their own thing instead of waiting for a payment.
